analysis.one_liner: Requires private insurance to cover new COVID-19 preventive services and vaccines within 15 business days instead of a year.
analysis.headline: Introduced with one cosponsor and referred to three committees, the bill never got a vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021 — but Congress enacted the same 15-business-day coverage rule a week after introduction in the CARES Act.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Affordable Care Act, health plans have up to a year to start covering a new preventive service once a federal expert panel recommends it. This bill would have cut that to 15 business days for any service or vaccine meant to prevent or diagnose COVID-19, once the US Preventive Services Task Force or the CDC's vaccine advisory committee recommended it. It also extended the requirement to grandfathered plans, which are normally exempt from this ACA mandate. The bill went to three House committees and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Insured Americans — people covered by employer plans, individual market plans, and grandfathered plans — would get new COVID-19 vaccines and preventive services covered free of copays and deductibles within 15 business days of a federal recommendation, instead of waiting up to a year. During a pandemic, that gap is the difference between a vaccine being free the month it is approved and people paying out of pocket or going uncovered through the worst of the outbreak.

how_it_helps.text: Insured people would get coverage of COVID-19 preventive services — an immunization recommended by the CDC's vaccine advisory committee or an A/B-rated service from the Preventive Services Task Force — within 15 business days, instead of waiting up to a year as under current law.
The bill explicitly applies the requirement to grandfathered health plans, which are otherwise exempt from the ACA preventive-services mandate, closing a gap in coverage.
Coverage would carry the same no-cost-sharing protection as other ACA preventive services, so patients would face no copay or deductible for the vaccine or service.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who sponsor group plans would pay the cost of covering the services with no patient cost-sharing, plus the administrative cost of adding benefits on two weeks' notice; those costs flow into premiums.

drawbacks.text: Under the Affordable Care Act, plans currently have up to a year to add newly recommended preventive services — time they use to update benefits, provider networks, and billing systems. A 15-business-day deadline, applied by all three relevant departments at once, could create implementation errors and coverage disputes for plans and doctor's offices alike.

The bill extends the no-cost-sharing mandate to grandfathered plans, which were deliberately exempted from that ACA requirement; those plans and the employers behind them would bear new costs, which could be passed back to enrollees through higher premiums.
The requirement applies only to private group and individual insurance; it does nothing for the uninsured, who had no guarantee of free COVID-19 vaccination under this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow and time-sensitive: insured people would get free COVID-19 vaccines and preventive care within two weeks of an expert recommendation instead of waiting up to a year, and grandfathered plans would no longer be exempt. The cost is higher premiums folded into what people already pay, plus a tight 15-business-day implementation window that plans and federal agencies would have to scramble to meet. On balance a reasonable emergency provision — and, notably, Congress agreed, adopting essentially the same rule in the CARES Act a week after this bill was introduced, which made the standalone bill moot.

outcome.mechanism: It sat with three House committees and never came up for a vote before the two-year Congress expired — though Congress passed the same 15-business-day coverage rule a week later in the CARES Act, so the idea became law anyway.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 19, 2020 and referred the same day to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor — and to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote. The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor over its lifetime, which usually signals a bill was not a legislative priority even among the sponsoring party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers were spared a standalone mandate for only days: Congress enacted the same 15-business-day COVID-19 coverage requirement in the CARES Act on March 27, 2020, so patients ultimately got the protection this bill sought, and the bill's sponsors could claim the idea carried.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, briefly — CARES Act covered it

for.name: Don Beyer

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no opposition is on the record; the bill simply never advanced past its committee referrals, with support limited to its two Democratic sponsors.

industries.note: The bill requires group and individual plans, including grandfathered ones, to cover new COVID-19 preventive services and vaccines with no patient cost-sharing within 15 business days of a recommendation. That front-loads costs that plans would otherwise have up to a year to absorb into premiums, and briefly pulls grandfathered plans into a mandate they were exempt from.

Employers with self-funded or grandfathered plans would face the accelerated coverage requirement and its costs, but their employees would get faster free access to COVID-19 protection, reducing illness and absenteeism.
Mandated rapid coverage with no patient cost-sharing makes it easier for people to say yes to a new COVID-19 vaccine or test, enlarging the market for the product faster.
